passage: Sunday afternoon in the flat, the pressure cooker hissed in the kitchen, and Ira lay on the sofa in her oldest T-shirt, scrolling. Pema on a beach at sunset. Pema holding a debate trophy. A classmate's perfect cake. Someone's new puppy. Every picture was brighter than Ira's whole week. She looked at her own last post: a blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago. Everyone's going somewhere, she thought, and I'm here with dal. She scrolled faster and felt worse. Then a message popped up from Pema herself: "Trip's been kind of awful tbh 😅 fought with my cousin, got sunburnt, want to come home." Ira read it twice. The sunset photo had gone up two hours ago.

qa.q: What was Ira's own last post?
qa.a: A blurry photo of rain on the balcony from a month ago.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling as she scrolled faster?
qa.a: She felt dull and left behind, as if everyone else was going somewhere while she was stuck at home with dal.

qa.q: After Pema's message, what could Ira choose to do with her scrolling?
qa.a: She could put the phone down, reply kindly to Pema, and remember that the sunset photo hid a bad day.

qa.q: What might Pema's day look like from Pema's side, compared with the photos?
qa.a: For Pema it was a fight, sunburn and missing home; the photo showed only one bright minute.

grounding: A teenager scrolling peers' polished photos feels dull and behind, until a friend's message shows what the highlights left out.

passage:
"Gopika, dinner. Why are you glaring at your phone like it owes you money?" Arnab dropped onto the bed.
"Everyone's life is better than mine. Look. Tanisha's at a music camp. Ritika got a new haircut and looks like a model. Even Mishti won something."
"And you?"
"I did a geography worksheet. Thrilling."
Arnab held out his own phone. "See this photo? Me on the hill at sunrise. Very cool, right?"
"Very cool."
"I'd been awake since three, I was freezing, and I threw up on the bus. I posted the one good second."
Gopika laughed despite herself. "Gross."
"Nobody posts their worksheet days, Gopu. You're putting your whole Tuesday next to their one best minute."
She put the phone face down. "Fine. What's for dinner?"
"Worksheet-level khichdi."
"Perfect."

qa.q: What had Gopika done that day?
qa.a: She did a geography worksheet.

qa.q: Why did Gopika feel her life was worse than everyone else's?
qa.a: Seeing camps, haircuts and prizes made her own worksheet day look dull by comparison.

qa.q: What did Arnab choose to share, and why did it work better than a lecture?
qa.a: He showed his own sunrise photo and told the freezing, sick truth behind it, so Gopika could see the gap herself and laugh 😅

qa.q: How does Arnab seem to see his sister's gloom?
qa.a: He takes it seriously but lightly, using his own story and a joke about khichdi to pull her back rather than scolding.

grounding: A teenager feels behind after scrolling peers' highlights, and her brother shows her the ordinary truth behind his own best photo.

passage: Last winter I had a habit I didn't notice was a habit. Every night in bed, I'd scroll. Dhruv at a coding contest, holding a certificate. Seniors at college fests. Someone from my old school who'd started a baking business at fifteen. I'd lie there with the screen lighting my face until Ma called, "Yogesh, lights off!", and think: I'm sixteen and I've done nothing. Then one day Dhruv came over to study, and I watched him fail the same maths problem four times, groan, and eat half a packet of biscuits. The certificate guy. He was just Dhruv, on a normal Tuesday. It sounds silly, but that's when I got it: I'd been holding my worst nights up against everyone's best photos. I still scroll sometimes. I just remember the biscuits.

qa.q: What was Dhruv holding in the photo?
qa.a: A certificate, at a coding contest.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling while scrolling in bed?
qa.a: Yogesh felt behind and worthless, thinking "I'm sixteen and I've done nothing."

qa.q: What was the turning point for Yogesh?
qa.a: Watching Dhruv fail the same maths problem four times and eat half a packet of biscuits, which showed the ordinary life behind the certificate.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel if he learned Yogesh had envied his certificate photo?
qa.a: Dhruv might be surprised, since on that normal Tuesday he was stuck on the same problem.

grounding: A teenager recalls feeling dull and behind while scrolling peers' achievements, until seeing a friend's ordinary day revealed they were only highlights.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10, Wednesday.
Anjali has seemed flat all week. During free period I found her in the library corner scrolling, not reading. On her screen: Anirban at a robotics camp, a cousin at a beach, a senior holding a trophy. Without looking up she said, "Everyone is doing something. I'm just... here." I asked what she had done since Sunday. She shrugged. Then, slowly: helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, finished a whole novel. I said none of those would ever make a photo. She almost smiled. Later I happened to see Anirban's caption under that camp picture: "Day 3, lost every round, so tired." None of that showed in the photo. I have invited Anjali to the Friday reading group, and I will check on her again on Monday.

qa.q: What had Anjali done since Sunday?
qa.a: Helped her grandmother with the pension forms, fixed the class projector, and finished a whole novel.

qa.q: What does Anjali's "I'm just... here" suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt dull and left behind, measuring her ordinary week against everyone else's highlights.

qa.q: Which move by the teacher helped most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Anjali had actually done since Sunday let her see her own week clearly, without a lecture about social media.

qa.q: How did Anirban's week at the camp really go, judging by the caption?
qa.a: By day 3 Anirban had lost every round and was very tired, so the glossy camp photo hid a hard, ordinary week, much like anyone's.

grounding: A teacher notices a student scrolling peers' polished posts and feeling dull and behind, and helps her see her own ordinary week beside their highlights.

passage:
Saturday, 11:40 pm
Should be asleep. Instead: forty minutes on Kiran's page. Kiran at the state quiz. Kiran's new haircut. Kiran's family at a hill station. Kiran with a certificate for something I didn't even know existed. My Saturday was maths tuition, washing my school shoes, and minding Chhotu so Mummy could nap. I feel like a grey sticker in a colourful album.
Then I remembered: last month I posted ONE photo, the cake I made for Papa's birthday. It looked perfect. Nobody saw the first cake, which sank in the middle and made Chhotu cry. So maybe Kiran's page is the second cake every time.
Still feel grey. Slightly less.
Phone is going in the drawer now.
Pooja

qa.q: What photo did Pooja post last month?
qa.a: The cake made for Papa's birthday.

qa.q: What does "a grey sticker in a colourful album" show about how Pooja feels?
qa.a: Pooja feels small and left out, as if an ordinary Saturday doesn't count next to Kiran's bright highlights.

qa.q: What thought changed the night, and what small choice followed?
qa.a: Remembering the sunken first cake made Pooja realise Kiran's page may show only the best versions too, and the phone went into the drawer.

qa.q: How might Kiran see that same page?
qa.a: Kiran knows the ordinary or failed moments behind each post and may have no idea anyone felt small looking at them.

grounding: A teenager scrolls a peer's highlights late at night, feels dull and behind, then remembers that posts show only the best moments.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday.
Manjula (class ten) came in today, low and teary. She said she spends two hours every night scrolling through classmates' pages. Pooja's especially: holidays in the hills, trophies, perfect family dinners. "My life is so boring. I'm behind at everything," she said. When I asked what she'd done that week, she listed a science project, helping her Nani, and a funny afternoon with her cousins. She hadn't counted any of it. We talked about how pages show the best moments, not the ordinary ones. She laughed a little when I asked if Pooja posted her bad hair days. We agreed she'll try muting a few accounts for a week and write down one good thing each night. Follow-up next Monday.

qa.q: How long does Manjula spend scrolling every night?
qa.a: She spends two hours every night scrolling through classmates' pages.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when she said her life was boring?
qa.a: Manjula felt low and behind, as if everyone else's life was brighter than hers.

qa.q: Why is writing down one good thing each night a helpful step?
qa.a: It helps Manjula notice her own ordinary good moments, instead of comparing them to others' highlights.

qa.q: How might Pooja's life look different offline?
qa.a: Pooja probably has boring and bad days too; her page just shows the best moments.

grounding: A teenager scrolling classmates' polished pages feels dull and behind, forgetting she only sees highlights, and a counsellor helps her notice her own days.

passage:
Thursday night
Scrolled for an hour again. Sunaina went to a concert in Mumbai, then posted a photo with her new guitar, then her science fair trophy. Everyone commented fire emojis and "queen."
I spent today doing algebra and eating rajma in my room.
I feel so dull. Like everyone is living a movie and I'm the background extra. I'm fifteen and haven't done ANYTHING.
Wait. Sunaina also told me last week she cried for two days because of her parents fighting. That wasn't on her page. Neither was the maths test she failed.
So I'm comparing my Thursday to her best moments. Of course I lose.
Putting the phone in the drawer. Going to practise my sketching instead.
- Tanuja

qa.q: What trophy did Sunaina post?
qa.a: She posted her science fair trophy.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel after scrolling?
qa.a: Tanuja felt dull and left behind, like the background extra in everyone else's movie.

qa.q: What did Tanuja realise, and why does it help?
qa.a: That Tanuja was comparing an ordinary Thursday to Sunaina's best moments, which explains the low feeling and loosens its hold.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel if she knew how her page affected Tanuja?
qa.a: Sunaina might be surprised, since her real life includes crying and failed tests that she never posts.

grounding: A teenager scrolling a friend's highlights feels dull and behind, then remembers the friend's hidden struggles and sees the unfair comparison.

In the small town of Bhilwara, the power was out and Zeenat lay on her bed with her phone at forty per cent. She opened the photo app.
Kiran, from her old school, was at a science camp in Bengaluru. Kiran at a beach. Kiran with a trophy. Kiran laughing with friends in matching T-shirts.
Zeenat looked around her room: the damp patch, the pile of Hindi notes, the same four walls. She felt heavy and dull, like her life was standing still.
She scrolled for an hour. The battery hit ten per cent.
Then her little brother came in with two cups of chai and a torch. "Ammi says come, the neighbours are singing on the roof." Zeenat hesitated, then put the phone down.

qa.q: Where was Kiran at a science camp?
qa.a: Kiran was at a science camp in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she looked around her room?
qa.a: She felt heavy, dull and behind, comparing her ordinary day with Kiran's highlight photos.

qa.q: What could Zeenat remind herself when scrolling next time?
qa.a: That she is seeing only Kiran's best moments, not her ordinary days, and that her own life has good moments like singing on the roof.

qa.q: What would change if Zeenat's brother hadn't come in?
qa.a: Zeenat might have kept scrolling and feeling worse, instead of joining a real moment with family and neighbours.

grounding: Shows a teenager scrolling a peer's polished photos and feeling dull and behind, forgetting she sees only highlights.

passage:
In Mexico City, Dalia sat on the metro scrolling. Alejandro, a boy from her class, had posted again: a violin concert, a medal from a maths contest, a trip to the coast with his cousins, a perfect breakfast.
Dalia looked at her reflection in the dark window: school uniform, tired eyes, a backpack full of homework. Everyone else seemed to be living; she was just getting through Tuesday.
At school, she saw Alejandro yawning at his desk. "Rough morning?" she asked.
"Terrible. I practised violin till midnight and I still messed up. My dad was really angry."
Dalia blinked. None of that was in the photos.

passage:
In the boarding school hostel, phones were allowed for one hour on Sunday. Ojas spent his whole hour scrolling.
Aditi, from his old day school, had posted photos from a national debate. Her certificate. A new haircut. A crowd of friends. Every post seemed to shine.
Ojas looked at his own week: dal-rice in the mess, a failed chemistry quiz, mud on his football boots. He felt like he was falling behind everyone.
When the hour ended, the housemaster collected the phones. He saw Ojas's face. "Bad news?"
"No. Just... everyone's doing better than me."
"Everyone's posting better than you," the housemaster said. "Different thing. Come, the match is starting."

qa.q: How long were phones allowed on Sunday?
qa.a: Phones were allowed for one hour on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as he looked at his own week?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and behind, comparing his ordinary week with Aditi's shining posts.

qa.q: How did the housemaster help Ojas?
qa.a: He pointed out that people post their best moments, and invited him to the match, pulling him back into real life.

qa.q: How might Aditi see her own week?
qa.a: Aditi's week probably had ordinary or hard moments too, which she didn't post.

grounding: Shows a teenager comparing his ordinary days to a peer's polished posts and feeling behind, and an adult reminding him posts are only highlights.

passage:
Dear Pooja Didi,
You asked why I've been quiet on calls. It's silly. Every night I scroll before sleeping and everyone's life looks amazing. Someone's at a science camp, someone got into a dance academy, someone's holiday photos are like a film. Then I look at my room with the fan that squeaks, and I feel so boring. Like I'm behind in a race nobody told me had started. Last Sunday I saw a girl from my class posting a perfect smiling photo. That same day she'd told me at tuition she was dreading her exam. So maybe I'm only seeing the best seconds of their weeks. I'm going to try keeping my phone outside my room this week. Tell me how your ordinary days go?
Arohi

qa.a: It squeaks.

qa.q: How does Arohi feel after scrolling each night?
qa.a: Arohi feels boring, discouraged and behind, as if in a race nobody announced, comparing an ordinary room with others' best moments.

qa.q: Is keeping the phone outside the room a good step? Why?
qa.a: Yes, because it breaks the nightly habit of comparing and gives Arohi space to remember that posts are highlights.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Pooja might feel protective and glad Arohi reached out, and may share honest stories of her own ordinary days.

passage: Okay, Divyansh, so you want to know why I deleted the app for a week? Here's what happened. Every night, I'd scroll. That girl from the other section with the perfect art. The guy who got into the national quiz. The cousin in Canada with snow and cafés. And I'd look at my own day, you know, maths homework and dal rice and my brother's cricket noise, and feel so dull. Like everyone was moving and I was stuck. Then last week you posted that picture from the beach trip, all smiles. And I remembered you'd been sick in the bus for two hours that day. I laughed so hard. And then I thought: oh. Everyone's showing me only the good second. So yeah, I, Sudha, am taking a break.

passage: Before: On a Friday night, Nikita scrolled for an hour. Farida from her class was at a music camp in the hills, posting sunsets. Nikita looked at her own weekend plan, which was chemistry revision, and felt flat and grey. She didn't reply to anyone. During: On Tuesday, at school, Farida was quiet at lunch. "The camp was hard," she admitted. "I cried the second night. I missed everyone." "But your photos..." "I only posted the good bits." Nikita sat back, surprised. After: The next Saturday, Nikita turned off the app notifications and revised in the park. She posted nothing. She felt fine. Better than fine, some moments.

qa.a: In the hills.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling while scrolling on Friday?

qa.a: Farida may feel relieved to be honest and less alone with the homesickness her photos hid.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling behind while scrolling peers' highlights, then learning they hide ordinary and hard moments.

passage: Saurabh, put the phone down for one minute and let your Jeevan chacha tell you something. The summer I was sixteen, Nagpur was forty-six degrees and I was stuck at home. Every night I lay under the fan scrolling. Rohit in Manali, in snow. Anjali at a science camp. Some boy from my class holding a guitar trophy. My life was power cuts and my mother's lauki. I felt so dull I stopped replying to anyone. Then in July Rohit came back. On the terrace he admitted the Manali trip was three days of car sickness and a fight with his dad; he had posted the one good photo. That night I understood: I had been comparing my every ordinary day with everyone's single best minute. So I started a small notebook of my own good minutes. Guess who still has it.

qa.q: How hot was Nagpur that summer?
qa.a: Forty-six degrees.

qa.q: How did young Jeevan feel while scrolling every night?
qa.a: He felt dull and left behind, so low that he stopped replying to anyone.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped young Jeevan?
qa.a: Starting a small notebook of his own good minutes, after realising he was comparing ordinary days with others' single best moments.

qa.q: What might Rohit have felt posting the one good photo from Manali?
qa.a: Rohit may have wanted to hide a disappointing trip and look happy, with private embarrassment behind the snowy picture.

grounding: A teenager scrolling friends' holiday highlights feels dull and behind until he sees he is comparing ordinary days with others' best moments.
